brief.question: What does the parliamentary record show about immigration?
brief.answer:
The most decision-relevant numbers in the record are about border control and visa enforcement. A government MP said Labor allowed more than 50,000 unauthorised boat arrivals, while John Howard left office with only four illegal maritime arrivals in detention; the same MP said the coalition then took back control, closed 19 detention centres, removed all children from detention, and saw boat arrivals fall from 800 under Labor to 34 interceptions under the Morrison government. Another coalition speaker contrasted visa cancellations of foreign criminals: 643 under Labor between 2008 and 2013 versus 5,023 under the coalition’s strengthened section 501 between December 2014 and December 2019. On the humanitarian side, a coalition senator claimed Australia’s refugee record was second only to Canada, with more than 100,000 refugees welcomed over 11 years, while a later government MP noted the offshore refugee program had been increased from 13,750 in 2013-14 to 18,750 in 2018-19, plus a special intake of 12,000 people fleeing Syria and Iraq.

The parliamentary record also tracks the composition and scale of migration. A coalition senator documented that skilled migration had grown from about 30 per cent of the intake after 1996 to around 70 per cent, with roughly 102,500 skilled places in the latest year, and argued this was important for the economy. Labor speakers, by contrast, said skilled migration should not be supported at the expense of apprenticeships and jobs for Australians. Opposition questioners more recently claimed record immigration is outpacing investment, driving declining productivity and exacerbating record homelessness, and criticised Labor for population growth while housing deals are announced.

Over time, the debate has shifted from bipartisan support for more humane detention policy to sharp partisan attacks and then back to claims of restored integrity. A committee report in December 2008, signed by the coalition shadow immigration minister, implicitly endorsed the Rudd government’s detention changes; a Labor senator said the committee found no evidence that detention policy deterred unlawful arrivals, noting only 304 unauthorised boat arrivals were in detention as of May 2009 and that Australia’s share of global asylum claims had averaged about 1.5 per cent over two decades. By 2009, opposition senators were instead citing UNHCR figures that Australian asylum applications rose over 25 per cent in nine months while global applications rose only five per cent, accusing Labor of an open-door policy. The coalition later framed its own record as restoring integrity to a “broken” system, arguing that strong borders were what allowed a bigger humanitarian program.

The sharpest disagreement is over cause and effect: Labor senators blamed “external factors such as natural disaster and conflict” for pushing boats and said the previous government’s detention policies were not a deterrent, while coalition members insisted Labor’s policy created “pull factors.” There is also a stark divide over transparency. A coalition MP said a 2012 Information Commissioner report into the immigration department under Labor exposed a “culture of cover-up and interference,” making the Prime Minister’s “let the sunshine in” promise hollow — even as government members accused the opposition of playing politics rather than governing.

On promises versus outcomes, the record contains a direct accusation against the Albanese government: before taking office it promised to cut immigration but instead delivered a record net migration result of more than 500,000 people a year, and only slowly wound it back toward a claimed target of 250,000. The government’s rebuttal, also in the record, is that the most recent data put net overseas migration around 17,000 below Treasury’s forecast for the first three quarters of 2024-25, that annual net migration had fallen for six consecutive quarters, and that it was over 40 per cent below its peak — because it was fixing a “broken, discredited, corrupted” system inherited from the coalition.

sections.question: What positions have MPs taken on asylum seekers and offshore detention?
sections.answer:
The strongest finding is that offshore detention has been a deeply divisive issue, with a clear majority in the Senate voting against ending it (39–9 on 15 February 2018), while a vocal cross-party minority, led by The Greens, has persistently pushed for its abolition and for bringing detainees to Australia.

**Positions in favour of ending offshore detention and bringing detainees to Australia:**
- **The Greens** are the only party committed to drastically improving Australia's approach, with Senator Nick McKim introducing a bill to evacuate all asylum seekers from offshore detention centres and bring them to Australia until safe, long-term options exist.
- **Independent MPs and crossbenchers** have strongly supported ending offshore detention. One MP (Kooyong) cited medical evidence, noting that "no-one is well after 10 years in offshore detention," and referenced a study showing 62% of 208 refugees assessed had moderate or severe depression, with 46 deaths in Australian detention centres over the last decade, including 12 offshore.
- **Ms Leong** condemned both Labor and Liberal governments for operating offshore detention on Manus Island and Nauru, calling conditions inhumane and contravening the UN refugee convention, and argued only The Greens support bringing all refugees to Australia.
- **A petition of over 60,000 signatures** was presented to parliament calling for an end to offshore detention, and **502 medical professionals** signed an open letter tabled in parliament calling for all consenting refugees and asylum seekers on Nauru and Papua New Guinea to be brought immediately to Australia.
- **The Refugee Protection Bill 2019** proposed abolishing mandatory detention and establishing a regional framework (APASS), criticising offshore detention as unlawful, inhumane, and costing $9.6 billion from 2013–2016.

**Positions in favour of maintaining offshore detention or regional processing:**
- **The government (Coalition)** defended offshore processing as a deterrent, citing the Houston report's 22 recommendations and passing legislation to establish offshore processing centres. A government speaker argued that detention capacity is needed for immigration management and that the vote was not about endorsing the Malaysia arrangement but about Migration Act amendments.
- **A Coalition MP** strongly defended offshore processing, arguing Australia should control who gets refugee places, that the Labor Party's shift to sending people to non-signatories of the UN convention was "morally contemptible," and that losing public confidence on border protection would be a "terrible step backwards."
- **The Senate majority (39 votes)** on 15 February 2018 voted against a motion to end offshore detention, including members of the Coalition, Labor, and crossbenchers such as Pauline Hanson, David Leyonhjelm, and Derryn Hinch.

**Historical and ongoing context:**
- In early 2019, parliament passed the "medevac" bill (with cross-party support and floor crossings) to evacuate critically sick detainees to Australia, but the previous Coalition government later repealed it.
- As of January 2023, about 500 offshore detainees lacked a durable solution, with 159 remaining in PNG or Nauru.
- A parliamentary question from November 2024 requesting a breakdown of asylum seekers transferred to Australia remained unanswered for one year and three months, indicating ongoing opacity.

sections.question: What has been said about immigration levels and skilled migration?
sections.answer:
Immigration policy debates have centred on the balance between skilled and unskilled intake, with the government defending its approach as economically essential and the opposition criticising it as mismanaged and too high.

**Government position:** The government argues skilled migration is vital for productivity and economic growth, particularly in regional areas. It highlights that skilled migrants now make up over two-thirds of the total intake, up from less than 30% under the Keating government. It points to a fourfold increase in skilled migrants settling in regional areas over the last decade and announces new measures like regional migration agreements and enterprise migration agreements. The government also notes it has increased English language requirements for skilled migrants and reduced the permanent migration program to 160,000 places, a 60% cut, to prioritise Australian workers. It rejects claims of record or uncontrolled immigration, citing census data, and stresses that migration is designed to produce unity, not division.

**Opposition and crossbench criticism:** Critics argue the government has "thrown the gates open" and failed to manage migration properly. They claim that only 20% of net overseas migrants in 2025 were skilled, with 80% unskilled, and that the skilled list includes questionable occupations like dog handler and golfer. They accuse the government of prioritising higher migration levels over Australian jobs and of bungling the response to the global financial crisis, waiting nine months to adjust skilled migration numbers. Some argue that low-skilled arrivals reduce wages for low-skilled Australian workers, while others contend that migration should not be attacked for the government's failure to invest in domestic skills training. The opposition also criticises the government for not clearly stating its position, with the shadow minister for immigration remaining silent on key initiatives.

**Independent and minor party views:** Some speakers defend skilled migration as an important component when administered properly, while warning against dangerous rhetoric that migrants take Australians' jobs. Others note that migration levels can be adjusted to economic circumstances and that a balanced intake is necessary for sustainable population levels.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Community safety and immigration?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on community safety and immigration was sharply partisan, with speakers trading accusations over the government's handling of detention, deportation and border policy. A Commonwealth speaker (whose party is not named in the passage) accused the Albanese Labor government of failure, saying that "more than 18 months after the parliament passed legislation to create the community safety order regime, the minister has still not lodged a single application for a preventive detention order," despite the member for Scullin promising in May last year that six applications were nearly ready and a further 26 were in an advanced stage. Another Commonwealth speaker claimed the government's failures included "the former minister for immigration's direction 99 debacle, which saw 97 criminal noncitizens avoid deportation," and that the Minister for Home Affairs had admitted "he had been personally interviewing Palestinian families before granting them humanitarian visas." The same speaker said the coalition supported the bill in question but had an amendment because "what we want to ensure is community safety," noting that "there are still 354 members roaming free in the Australian community who are members of the so-called NZYQ cohort," which "includes rapists, paedophiles, murderers and a contract killer."

Other Commonwealth speakers defended the government's approach. One said "community safety is our number one priority – not politics, not headlines, but safety," and argued that "strong powers must come with strong safeguards" and that "ministerial discretion must be exercised transparently and responsibly." A Victorian minister (whose party is not named in the passage) rejected a motion from the Liberal Party, saying it showed "how low Jess Wilson and the Liberal Party are willing to go to cosy up to Pauline Hanson and to One Nation," and accused the federal Liberal Party of failing to condemn "the hateful anti-Muslim comments of Pauline Hanson or the anti-Indian comments of Jacinta Price or the anti-immigration comments of Angus Taylor." That minister stressed that "no multicultural community is served by polarisation and division" and that "it is measured, thoughtful leadership that keeps communities safe and united, not whipping up fear."

A Commonwealth speaker from Kooyong said their community had "grave concerns around the precedent set by this piece of legislation," while acknowledging that "all of us care about keeping Australians safe" and that the government must "deal fairly and justly with some of the most consequential decisions that a government can make—decisions about the deportation, detention and transfer of vulnerable individuals." Another Commonwealth speaker argued that "confusing and legitimate concerns in the community about high immigration" with racism "is wrong," and that such concerns "shouldn't be an excuse to shut down legitimate debates." A speaker in the New South Wales Parliament (The Entrance) addressed the Terrorism and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2025, saying the events of 14 December at Bondi, where "15 people of the Jewish faith" were killed, "demand that we reconvene... to do all we can within the walls of this Parliament to make our communities safer." The record on this question is otherwise limited, with some passages touching only briefly on related themes such as social cohesion, anti-vilification laws and the need for parliamentary scrutiny of migration legislation.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Multicultural Victoria Amendment Bill 2026?
sections.answer:
Debate on the Multicultural Victoria Amendment Bill 2026 was extensive and largely bipartisan in the Victorian Parliament, with the bill abolishing the Victorian Multicultural Commission and establishing a new statutory entity, Multicultural Victoria, led by a multicultural coordinator general. The coalition did not oppose the bill's second reading, with Shadow Assistant Minister for Multicultural and Multifaith Affairs Mr Mulholland saying the change "could provide a more coordinated whole-of-government response to concerns raised by communities" and noting "welcome accountability measures," but he moved amendments over concerns including the timing of appointments, the lack of a guaranteed dedicated workforce or operating budget, and the need for meaningful multifaith representation. The Libertarian Party opposed the bill entirely, with one member arguing "the government does not need to be interfering in this" and that the preferred-provider model for VITS LanguageLoop "is actually destroying market diversity." Legalise Cannabis Victoria supported the bill, and the Greens supported it in principle while moving amendments, with one Greens member criticising that the bill "does not even mention racism or discrimination" and arguing the government had shown "utter disregard for genuine good-faith consultation" with the language services sector.

Government speakers strongly defended the bill. Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny tabled statements of compatibility with the Charter of Human Rights and the Statewide Treaty Act 2025, describing the bill as "a fundamentally rights-promoting piece of legislation." Minister Ingrid Stitt, in her second-reading speech, said the bill "delivers on key commitments arising from the Review" led by George Lekakis AO and that Multicultural Victoria "signals a reset in how we as a government listens to, collaborates with and supports multicultural and multifaith Victorians." Several Labor members spoke in support, including the member for Greenvale, who said "multiculturalism and national unity are not opposites," and the member for Narre Warren South, who said the bill ensures "the security of our multicultural institutions" against a potential "Liberal–One Nation coalition." Opposition members, including the member for Warrandyte, accused Labor of politicising multiculturalism, saying "we will not tolerate the racism from Labor or the politicisation of multiculturalism from Labor," while the member for South Eastern Metropolitan said the new structure would be "fully controlled by the government" and that "it is already too political."

sections.question: What has parliament said about Australian Indian Community and immigration?
sections.answer:
The New South Wales Parliament debated a motion acknowledging the contribution of the Indian Australian community and rejecting criticism of migration from India. Mr Warren Kirby (Riverstone), who moved the motion, said the community has "among the highest rates of employment and the lowest rates of incarceration" and that their values "are perfectly aligned with Australian values". Mr Mark Speakman (Cronulla, Liberal) said over 200,000 people born in India call New South Wales home, that Indian-born residents are "Australia's second largest taxpaying migrant group", and that two-way trade has reached "over $24 billion annually". Mr Mark Coure (Oatley, Liberal) said more than 350,000 people of Indian ancestry live in New South Wales.

The debate was sparked by comments from federal Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price, which multiple speakers condemned. Mr Kirby said her comments were "appalling and have caused deep hurt for our Australian Indian community", and Mr Coure said they were "not only wrong but deeply hurtful". Mr Speakman said the NSW Liberals and Nationals were "sorry for the deep hurt many Indian Australians feel" after the Senator's comments. Ms Donna Davis (Parramatta, Labor) quoted a local student who said "to hear our vote was bought is simply disrespectful". Mr Stephen Kamper (Rockdale, Labor), the Minister for Multiculturalism, said the March for Australia's claim about migration numbers was "a blatant falsehood peddled by those with ulterior motives". Mr Kirby also noted that "Australia's migration rate has consistently been maintained at approximately 1 per cent of the total population".

The Commonwealth Parliament also addressed the issue. A government speaker said "targeting specific ethnic groups, like the wave of anti-Indian sentiment that we saw over the weekend, is racism—full stop", and that "No-one in Australia should have to justify their belonging in this country". Another speaker noted that "the scapegoating of Indian communities, designed to undermine their sense of safety and belonging, is wrong". A Victorian Parliament speaker, discussing attacks on the Indian community, said "you belong" and that "Our new Australians living in Victoria could have chosen to live anywhere in the world. They chose us."

sections.question: What has parliament said about Bondi Beach Terrorist Incident and immigration?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on the Bondi Beach terrorist incident was extensive and highly partisan, with speakers from multiple parties and parliaments addressing the attack and its aftermath. The Hon. Mark Latham (NSW Legislative Council) argued that the political class was "culpable in allowing the radical Islamic terrorism of Naveed and Sajid Akram to strike at Bondi," criticising both the Coalition for allowing Sajid Akram into the country under the Howard Government with "inadequate security checking processes" and those who failed to address Islamic hate preachers. He claimed the government had been "banning everything except for the big one that truly matters: Islamic hate preachers and the terrorism they promote," and questioned why a neo-Nazi could be deported but not "these Islamic hate preachers in Western Sydney urging the murder of innocent people." sections.question: What positions have MPs taken on asylum seekers and offshore detention since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Positions on asylum seekers and offshore detention were sharply critical from several MPs, with Labor and the coalition accused of colluding against asylum seekers. One senator claimed: "What we are seeing here is the continuation of a decade-long collusion between the Labor Party and the coalition to destroy the lives of people who seek asylum in this country," adding that the offshore prison on Manus Island held "well north of a thousand people" who were "black- or brown-skinned" and not a single white person. Another senator said the government and coalition "agreed to ram through" a bill "to strip natural justice, a fundamental right, from asylum seekers and whomever else the government chooses to deport to Nauru," and described offshore detention as "a system that the UK government toyed with copying from us but abandoned, because it was just too inhumane." A third MP characterised offshore detention as emerging "during a period of toxic politics that saw a race to the bottom on how to treat people seeking asylum," noting that people were "forced, coerced and deceived into going to so called 'regional processing countries.'"

Other MPs highlighted the human and financial costs. One senator noted that "spending on offshore processing has blown out to $12.1 billion since offshore detention was started in 2012, with $580 million to Nauru in the 2025-26 budget," and questioned how the department justifies "the warehousing of people who are seeking asylum offshore at this cost, in breach of international obligations and to the detriment of their health and welfare." In the New South Wales parliament, Ms Jenny Leong praised volunteers and organisations supporting asylum seekers, including Professor Mark Harris, who "for the past 25 years has provided vital medical care to people seeking asylum," and House of Welcome, which has "always supported clients to navigate broken systems and campaigned for lasting policy change." In the Commonwealth parliament, Mr Jihad Dib, a Labor MP, commended Settlement Services International for providing services to migrants and asylum seekers, but the record also shows repeated frustration in Senate estimates over unanswered questions about asylum seekers transferred to offshore detention, with one senator noting a question from 4 November 2024 had gone "one year and three months" without an answer.

sections.question: What has been said about immigration levels and skilled migration since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Debate on immigration levels and skilled migration was sharply partisan. Government speakers, including a representative from the Department of Home Affairs, highlighted measures to strengthen integrity in the international education sector, the closure of the business innovation and investment program on 31 July 2024, and the implementation of the new national innovation visa and skills-in-demand visa in December 2024. They noted "very strong growth in demand" for the skills-in-demand visa, with 164,860 applications in 2024-25 compared to 121,168 previously. A Labor senator argued that "we do not have record levels of immigration" and that Australia "desperately rely[ies] on immigration" for essential services, citing Jobs and Skills Australia data showing unmet labour demand in health care, education, construction and utilities. Another government senator stated net overseas migration "has now fallen for six quarters in a row in annual terms, and it's over 40 per cent down on its peak," attributing this to fixing the "broken, discredited, corrupted immigration system" inherited from the coalition.

Opposition speakers strongly criticised the government's record. One senator claimed net overseas migration was 315,900 for the year to 31 March 2025, "46 per cent higher than the 10-year average before the COVID-19 pandemic," and accused Labor of "flooding the market with record net overseas migration." Another asserted that "just 20 per cent of your 301,000 net overseas migrants in 2025 were skilled" and that the skilled list included occupations such as "dog handler, hairdresser, gardener, golfer and migration agent." A coalition senator said between 2022 and 2023 the government brought in 737,000 migrants but only 51,605 had skills, of whom only 1,800 were from construction. The same speaker criticised the Temporary Skilled Migration Income Threshold, which rose from $53,900 under the previous government to $70,000 on 1 July 2023, then to $73,150 in July 2024 and $76,515 in July 2025, pricing out employers in dairy, horticulture and meat under labour agreements. Another opposition senator noted the government had not announced the 2025-26 permanent migration program by mid-August 2025, causing issues for skilled independent stream applicants.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Anti-Immigration Protests?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on the anti-immigration protests was sharply partisan. In the Queensland parliament, an opposition MP described the government as "mediocre, immature" and accused the Premier of failing to "publicly condemn the anti-immigration protests," while claiming the Deputy Premier "defended the protests." The same MP said the LNP "seek to use multicultural communities as a political battering ram." A Labor MP responded that "No-one from the government came out to call those out—not one," and accused the government of refusing to condemn "the racism we saw outside at the rallies on 31 August," while urging the Premier to "call it out and also put One Nation last."

In the Commonwealth parliament, the Greens moved a motion that "Condemns the racist, white supremacist, and anti-immigrant rallies held over the weekend and condemns the support of and attendance at the rallies by MPs." Greens Senator Nick McKim criticised the Labor government for "ramming through legislation that targets multicultural Australia" and for joining "with Peter Dutton to pass those hateful laws," while also condemning "the senators and MPs who supported and spoke at the marches." Labor's Minister for Multicultural Affairs described the marchers as "blatantly racist" and having an "anti-immigration agenda," and a government senator said the Prime Minister's government "stands with all Australians, no matter where they were born, against those who seek to divide us and intimidate migrant communities," calling the targeting of specific ethnic groups "racism—full stop."

Other speakers offered contrasting views. Liberal Senator Paul Scarr said many in the community were "extremely disappointed by the sight of Neo-Nazis on the steps of the Victorian parliament," but argued the issues must be discussed in a "considered, measured and reasoned" way. One senator, in a passage that appears to be from a different speaker, claimed the protests "are not about religion, skin colour or past nationality. They're about mass immigration," saying it was "about the numbers swamping our country, housing and homelessness." A First Nations senator said "no colonial government in this country has the right to say who and who isn't illegal on stolen land," and told people "you are welcome here and you are not alone."

eras.label: 1993–2009
eras.question: How did parliament argue about immigration between 1993 and 2009? The debates of the period included Australian Citizenship Amendment (Citizenship Testing) Bill 2007, Auditor-General’s Reports and Migration Amendment (Abolishing Detention Debt) Bill 2009.
eras.answer:
Debate on immigration in this period was sharply partisan, with speakers clashing over the balance between border security and humane treatment. On the Migration Amendment (Abolishing Detention Debt) Bill 2009, government supporters framed it as correcting a "significant social injustice" and ending "a policy that penalises persons who come to our shores seeking asylum from persecution in their homelands." One speaker called the detention debt "an arbitrary and pointless policy—a policy that makes Australia the only country in the world that charges innocent people the cost of incarcerating them." The same speaker argued that "fair and effective immigration detention policies and strong border security measures" are not incompatible, and that the bill achieved balance by still requiring "convicted illegal foreign fishers and people smugglers" to pay their debts.

Opposition speakers rejected this framing. One claimed the bill showed the Rudd government failing on "national security" and "economic management," areas where the former Howard government had succeeded. Another speaker, while agreeing with Senator Cormann on some issues, disagreed with him on this bill, and the record shows the Greens opposed a motion to discharge the bill from the Notice Paper, wanting it kept for debate.

On the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Citizenship Testing) Bill 2007, the debate centred on whether a citizenship test promoted inclusion. One speaker said the test was "a very exclusionary measure" despite its stated aim of a "more inclusive society," since "tests are, by their very nature, designed to be passed or failed." Another noted the Senate Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs had heard evidence that "Australia has been well served by its existing, inclusive citizenship laws" and that no case had been made for changing them. The record also shows committee recommendations for reviewing the testing regime's impact on refugee and humanitarian entrants, and for the test questions to be tabled in parliament.

eras.label: 2010–2019
eras.question: How did parliament argue about immigration between 2010 and 2019? The debates of the period included Racism and Harmony Day.
eras.answer:
Debate over immigration in this period was frequently framed through the lens of racism, multiculturalism and Harmony Day, with sharp partisan conflict over the Racial Discrimination Act. A Labor MP for Perth, Patrick Gorman, attacked the then Coalition government for seeking to weaken section 18C, claiming the Prime Minister introduced the amendment on Harmony Day and that the Liberal Party had an "appeasement policy towards Pauline Hanson 2.0". He argued that weakening the law would harm ethnic communities and that "racism, wherever it occurs, does not just harm its direct victims; rather, it demeans us all". In the New South Wales Legislative Council, Labor's Daniel Mookhey supported a Coalition motion on Harmony Day, noting the day marks the UN International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination and that the Christchurch massacre the week prior was "a pertinent reminder as to why it is so important that we remain vigilant against racism in all its forms". He also said Labor had been "campaigning for a toughening of the law relating to hate speech".

Other speakers echoed these themes. A Labor MP for the Commonwealth seat of Chifley, Ed Husic, described Harmony Day as more than food and clothing, arguing it is "about respect" and "promoting substantive equality by eliminating barriers to participation for all people". He criticised the government for proposing changes to 18C on the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, saying the government was "beholden to the far right on its backbench". A Labor MP for Hindmarsh, Steve Georganas, similarly condemned the government for discussing watering down 18C on Harmony Day, calling it "an absolute disgrace". In the Commonwealth parliament, Labor MP Tim Watts spoke of the return of "race based politics" in 2018, citing a former Coalition Prime Minister calling for an immigration policy "seemingly intended to discriminate against black African migrants" and warning that "the leadership void" at the heart of government had been "filled by extremists who want to sabotage and destroy Australia's multicultural success story". He also noted that 85 per cent of Australians supported multiculturalism according to the Scanlon Foundation. The record also includes a question to a Labor minister, Kate Lundy, in the Commonwealth Senate, who described Harmony Day as a day to celebrate cultural diversity with the message "Everyone belongs".

eras.label: 2020–2024
eras.question: How did parliament argue about immigration between 2020 and the middle of 2024? The debates of the period included South Australian Multicultural Bill, Afghanistan and COVID-19.
eras.answer:
Debate on immigration in this period was largely conducted through the South Australian Multicultural Bill 2020, with speakers from multiple parties. A Labor member, the lead speaker for the opposition, said the bill would "advance multiculturalism and interculturalism in South Australia" and noted the opposition supported its modernising intent but had three outstanding amendments: recognising temporary migrants' contribution, making "raising awareness of the harm that racism can do" a commission function, and requiring state authorities to report on the charter to parliament. Another Labor member, speaking on the same bill, said Labor supported updating the act and that its amendments would "strengthen the role of the proposed South Australian multicultural commission by ensuring grassroots community representation". A government member, who said his grandparents migrated from Madeira, commended the bill, noting it reflected consultation feedback including that "Aboriginal South Australians should be recognised as the carriers of the original cultures in South Australia". A different government member, the minister for multicultural affairs, later said the government had delivered on a "historic multicultural policy", including reinstating a Multicultural Women's Leadership course and establishing a Multicultural Chambers of Commerce group.

A separate debate concerned Afghanistan and refugees. A Labor member moved a motion calling on the Morrison government to grant Afghan nationals on temporary visas a path to permanent residency, facilitate migration for those who worked with Australian forces, and increase family reunion visas. He said South Australia had "an incredibly proud record of really leading the nation when it comes to multiculturalism" and described individuals on Safe Haven Enterprise visas who faced uncertainty, quoting one as saying, "I have lived here for 10 years. We have some freedom, but we still don't have the same freedoms as others." A government minister, responding to a question about COVID-19 and multicultural communities, said the home quarantine trial with South Australia would allow families to be reunited, "particularly those in our multicultural communities across this country who have carried the hardest and heaviest burden of that international ban". Another government minister, answering a question about COVID-19 testing, said there had been misunderstandings among culturally and linguistically diverse communities, including that non-citizens without Medicare might be charged for tests, and stressed that "anybody who presents for a COVID test will have it free of charge".

key_moments.title: Australian Citizenship Bill 2005; Australian Citizenship (Transitionals and Consequentials) Bill 2005
key_moments.speaker: Ian Campbell
key_moments.brief: The Australian Citizenship Bill 2005 was introduced to replace the 1948 Act, retaining citizenship as a privilege and adding a four-year lawful residence requirement (including 12 months as a permanent resident), mandatory refusal for security threats, identity verification, and new revocation grounds, with several recommendations from the Senate committee adopted. The companion Australian Citizenship (Transitionals and Consequentials) Bill 2005 implements transitional arrangements, including applying the new residence rules only to future permanent residents and registering adoptions under the Hague Convention.

key_moments.title: Migration Amendment (Notification Review) Bill 2008
key_moments.speaker: Stephen Conroy
key_moments.brief: The Migration Amendment (Notification Review) Bill 2008 was introduced to clarify how the Department of Immigration, Migration Review Tribunal, and Refugee Review Tribunal communicate with clients. It aims to address notification defects that have caused court challenges, unlawful detention, and large legacy caseloads, including changes regarding minors, substantial compliance with notification content, and deemed versus actual receipt.

key_moments.brief: The Migration Amendment (Detention Reform and Procedural Fairness) Bill 2010 was moved to end offshore processing and excision, make detention a last resort, end indefinite detention, and introduce judicial review of detention beyond 30 days, citing Australia's international obligations and a High Court ruling that asylum seekers on excised territory must receive procedural fairness.

lede.text:
Parliament argued sharply over community safety and immigration, with Commonwealth speakers accusing Labor of failing to lodge a single preventive detention order and of the "direction 99 debacle, which saw 97 criminal noncitizens avoid deportation," while defenders insisted "community safety is our number one priority."

From 1993 to 2009 parliament clashed over detention debt and citizenship testing as exclusionary. In the 2010s debate turned on racism, section 18C and Harmony Day. By 2020–24 attention shifted to multicultural commissions and Afghan refugees. The tide of attention has stayed roughly level across the decades.

Thirty per cent of Australians were born overseas, against a 14 per cent OECD average, and skilled migrants add $198,000 each in budget contribution. Labor defends falling net migration; the Liberals back caps and skilled prioritisation; the Greens oppose offshore detention; Katter disputes One Nation-style claims.
